Memorandum of Association

The objects of the company

The memorandum names seven objects for which the company is established. Each is listed here as lettered in the document.

A

Agriculture and general merchandise

To engage in general merchandise and carry on the business of agriculture in all its branches, including crop cultivation, livestock farming, fishery, poultry and other allied activities for commercial purposes.

B

Processing and marketing

To engage in the processing, packaging, storage, distribution and marketing of agricultural produce, livestock and food products, both locally and internationally.

C

Farm inputs supply

To provide agricultural supply of farm inputs, such as fertilizers, agrochemicals, machinery and other related equipment, to farmers and organizations.

D

Land, machinery and equipment

To purchase, lease or acquire any land, machinery or equipment necessary or convenient for the company's agricultural operations.

E

Borrowing and security

To borrow or raise money for the purpose of the company's business and to secure repayment in any manner the company may think fit.

F

Partnerships and arrangements

To enter into arrangements or partnerships with individuals, companies or government bodies that may seem conducive to the company's objectives.

G

Incidental powers

To do all such other things as are incidental or conducive to the attainment of the above objects or any of them.

How the business is set up

Built to operate and grow

The company's governing documents give it the structure, funding and reach to run a full agricultural business.

Management

Run by its directors

Directors are responsible for the company's business and may delegate powers to committees or individuals. Decisions are recorded in writing and kept for at least 10 years.

Capital to start, power to borrow

The company may borrow or raise money for its business, secure repayment, and buy or lease the land, machinery and equipment its farms need.

Articles of Association

How the company is run

The articles follow the Companies and Allied Matters Act, 2020. Open a group to see its main rules in plain language.

Directors and their decisions

Meetings, voting, appointment and pay
Collective decisions

Directors decide by majority at a meeting or by a unanimous written decision. A sole director may decide alone.

Meetings and quorum

Any director can call a meeting with notice of the date, time and place. The quorum is two where there are up to six directors, and one third above that.

Chair and casting vote

Directors may appoint a chairman, who holds a casting vote on a tie. If the chair is absent after one hour, those present choose one of themselves.

Conflicts of interest

A director with an interest in a proposed transaction is not counted for quorum or voting, with limited exceptions.

Records

Written records of every directors' decision are kept for at least 10 years.

Appointment and ending of office

Directors are appointed by ordinary resolution, or by the directors to fill a casual vacancy. Office ends on bankruptcy, incapacity, legal prohibition or resignation.

Remuneration and expenses

Directors receive the pay the company decides, and reasonable expenses for meetings and their duties are covered.

Alternate directors

A director may appoint an alternate to act in their absence, by written notice. The alternate is liable for their own acts.

Shares and distributions

Dividends, certificates, transfers, calls and forfeiture
Dividends

Declared by ordinary resolution on the directors' recommendation, never above the amount they recommend. Directors may pay interim dividends.

Payment

By bank transfer, cheque to the registered address, or another agreed means. No interest is paid unless the share terms say so.

Unclaimed sums

The directors may invest unclaimed dividends for the company. After twelve years unclaimed, the right to them ends.

Capitalising profits

With an ordinary resolution, directors may turn profits or reserves into new fully paid shares or debentures for the people entitled.

Issuing shares

No share is issued below its nominal value and any premium. Different classes, including redeemable shares, may be created by ordinary resolution.

Certificates

Every shareholder gets certificates free of charge, with replacements for damaged or lost ones.

Transfers and transmission

Shares move by instrument of transfer. Directors may refuse to register a transfer and must return it with notice. Heirs and trustees may take up or pass on shares.

Lien, calls and forfeiture

The company has a lien on partly paid shares. Call notices give at least 14 days. Unpaid calls can lead to forfeiture, and members may surrender shares as a gift.

Decisions by shareholders

General meetings, voting, polls and proxies
Attending meetings

Members may attend, speak and vote from different places so long as they can take part live. Directors may always attend and speak.

Chairing

The appointed chairman presides. Otherwise the directors present do, or the meeting appoints a director or shareholder as its first business.

Adjournment

A meeting without a quorum after one hour must adjourn. A new notice is needed if it resumes more than 30 days later.

Voting

Resolutions pass on a show of hands unless a poll is demanded. Electronic meetings may vote electronically.

Polls

A poll can be demanded by the chairman, three members, or members holding at least one tenth of the voting rights or paid-up capital.

Proxies

A proxy is appointed by written notice that names the shareholder and the meeting. It can be revoked before the meeting starts.

Amending resolutions

An ordinary resolution may be amended with 48 hours' written notice. A special resolution may be amended only to fix a non-substantive error.

Administration

Notices, seals, borrowing, indemnity and insurance
Communication

Documents may be sent in any way CAMA 2020 allows, including electronically. A director may agree a shorter deemed delivery time.

Company seal

Used only with the directors' authority, and signed by an authorised person with a witness.

Inspection of records

Shareholders cannot inspect accounts or records merely by being shareholders, unless the law, the directors or an ordinary resolution allows it.

Borrowing powers

Directors may borrow for the business, mortgage or charge its property and uncalled capital, and issue debentures and other securities.

Employees on closure

Directors may provide for current and former employees when the business ceases or is transferred.

Indemnity and insurance

Directors may be indemnified out of company assets where the law allows, and the company may buy insurance for their benefit.

Liability of members

Each member's liability is limited to any amount unpaid on the shares they hold.
